sections.text:
John is on an island called Patmos, a prisoner. It is the Lord’s day, and behind him a loud voice sounds like a trumpet. He turns and sees seven golden lamp stands, and among them one like a son of man, with eyes like a flame of fire. John falls at his feet like a dead man. A hand rests on him, and a voice says, “Don’t be afraid.”

So begin the visions. First come messages to seven churches. Then John is shown the throne of God and a Lamb who was slain, and a series of judgments pictured as seals, trumpets and bowls. The book sets the conflict between God and the powers of evil before the reader as a dragon, beasts and the city Babylon.

Then the scene changes. Christ returns, the final judgment comes, and John sees a new heaven and a new earth. A voice says that God will dwell with his people, “He will wipe away every tear from their eyes.” And the one on the throne says, “I am making all things new.”

The book names its writer as John, on Patmos. It is usually dated to the mid 90s, under the emperor Domitian. Some date it to the 60s, under Nero. It belongs to a kind of writing that speaks through symbols and numbers, and it draws constantly on the Old Testament.

Christians read Revelation in four main ways. Some see it as mostly about the first century. Some take it as a map of church history. Some see it as mostly about events still to come. And some read it as a picture of the struggle between good and evil in every age. They also differ on the thousand years of chapter 20.

All of them agree on its core: God and the Lamb win, and the churches are called to stay faithful.

An old man is on an island called Patmos, and he says he is there because of God's Word and the testimony of Jesus. On the Lord's day, he is in the Spirit, and behind him he hears a loud voice like a trumpet telling him to write what he sees and to send it to seven assemblies in Asia.

He turns. He sees seven golden lamp stands, and among them one like a son of man, with hair white as wool, eyes like fire, a voice like many waters, and a face like the sun shining at its brightest. John falls at his feet like a dead man.

A hand is laid on him. “I am the first and the last,” the voice says, and the one who was dead is alive forever and holds the keys of Death and of Hades. He tells John to write what he has seen, what is, and what will happen after.

Revelation is usually dated to the end of the first century, when Christians in Asia were under pressure; tradition links it to the apostle John, while some scholars think it was written by another John. It is written in the style of prophecy and apocalyptic, with many symbols. Christians read it in different ways: some see events of the first century, some a sweep of history, some events still to come, and some a picture that applies in every age.

Four letters, four towns, and one voice behind them all. Christ speaks to the assembly in Ephesus: I know your toil and perseverance, and you've tested false apostles. But “you left your first love”. Remember where you fell from, repent, do the first works.

To Smyrna he says he knows their oppression and poverty, though they are rich. Don't be afraid of what you are about to suffer. Be faithful to death and he will give the crown of life.

To Pergamum he says they hold firmly to his name even where Satan's throne is, and mentions Antipas, his witness, who was killed among them. But some hold the teaching of Balaam and the Nicolaitans.

To Thyatira he praises their love, faith, service and endurance, but speaks against a woman called Jezebel who leads his servants astray.

Each letter ends the same way: let those who have an ear hear what the Spirit says, and each promises something to the one who overcomes: the tree of life, escape from the second death, hidden manna and a white stone, authority over the nations and the morning star.

These are the first four of seven letters to real congregations in Asia, and each follows a pattern: a title for Christ, what he knows, what he holds against them, a call to hear and a promise. Verse 9 speaks of a synagogue of Satan. That phrase belongs to a conflict between two groups who both claimed the heritage of Israel, and it has been tragically misused against Jews. It is not a judgment on the Jewish people.

The letters go on. To Sardis: you have a reputation of being alive, but you are dead. Wake up and strengthen what remains. A few there have not defiled their garments, and they will walk with Christ in white.

To Philadelphia, a small and faithful assembly: I have set before you an open door, which no one can shut. You have a little power, but you kept my word and did not deny my name. Because you kept my command to endure, I will keep you in the hour of testing.

Then the last, to Laodicea, and it is the sharpest. He says they are “neither cold nor hot”, and that he will spit them out of my mouth. You say you are rich and need nothing, yet you are wretched, poor, blind and naked. Those I love, I reprove and chasten.

And then the door. “Behold, I stand at the door and knock.” If anyone hears and opens, I will come in and dine with him, and he with me. The one who overcomes will sit with him on his throne.

These are the last three of the seven letters. The phrase synagogue of Satan returns in verse 9, and the note under chapter 2 applies here too: it belongs to a first century conflict and must not be turned against Jewish people today. Christians read the knock at the door in two ways, as a call to a whole assembly that has grown comfortable, and as an invitation to any individual, and both readings are held widely.

A door stands open in heaven. John hears the same trumpet-like voice that spoke to him before: Come up here, and I will show you what must happen after this. Immediately he is in the Spirit, and there is a throne, and someone sitting on it who looks like jasper and sardius. A rainbow, like an emerald, surrounds the throne.

Around it sit twenty-four elders in white with golden crowns. Lightnings, sounds and thunders come from the throne, and seven lamps of fire burn before it. In front of it lies something like a sea of glass, like crystal.

Four living creatures, full of eyes, stand in the middle of the throne and around it: one like a lion, one like a calf, one with a face like a man, and one like a flying eagle. Each has six wings. They never rest, day or night, saying “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God, the Almighty”.

And whenever they give glory, the elders fall down, throw their crowns before the throne, and worship the one who lives forever, because he created all things.

After the letters to the seven assemblies on earth, the scene moves to heaven, to a throne room where worship goes on. The images draw on Old Testament visions of God's throne, such as Isaiah 6 and Ezekiel 1 and 10. Christians differ about who the twenty-four elders are: some see representatives of the people of God, others angelic beings. The chapter sets the stage for the scroll in chapter 5.

In the right hand of the One on the throne lies a scroll, written inside and outside and sealed with seven seals. A mighty angel calls out: who is worthy to open it? No one in heaven or on earth or under the earth is able. And John weeps much.

One of the elders says to him, Don't weep. The Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has overcome, and he can open the scroll. John looks for a lion. What he sees is a Lamb, standing as though it had been slain, in the middle of the throne.

The Lamb takes the scroll, and heaven erupts. The living creatures and the elders fall down with harps and golden bowls of incense and sing a new song about being bought for God out of every tribe, language, people and nation. Then the voice of many angels, ten thousands of ten thousands, cries out, “Worthy is the Lamb who has been killed”.

And last, every created thing joins in, to the One on the throne and to the Lamb.

The chapter turns on a surprise: the Lion that is announced turns out to be a Lamb that has been slain. Christians generally see this as the way Jesus is both king and sacrifice, and connect the Lamb with John 1:29 and Isaiah 53. What the scroll holds is read in several ways, such as God's plan for history or the coming judgments, and the opening of its seals begins in chapter 6.

The Lamb opens the first seal, and a voice like thunder says, “Come and see!” Out comes a white horse, its rider holding a bow and wearing a crown. With the second seal a red horse rides out, and its rider is given a great sword and the power to take peace from the earth. The third is a black horse with a balance, and a voice calls out the price of wheat and barley. The fourth is pale, the rider is named Death, and Hades follows him.

Then the scene turns. Under the altar are the souls of those killed for the Word of God, and they cry out, “How long, Master,” until justice comes. Each is given a white robe and told to rest a little longer. The sixth seal shakes the earth and the sky, and everyone from kings to slaves hides in the rocks, asking, “who is able to stand?”

This is John’s vision, written for the Christian assemblies of his day. The seals are the first of three series of sevens in the book, followed by trumpets and bowls. Christians read the four horsemen in different ways: as events in the first-century world, as pressures that return in every age, or as events still to come. The cry of the martyrs is a prayer made in the middle of suffering. Nothing is opened until the Lamb opens it (see Revelation 5).

Everything holds its breath. Four angels stand at the four corners of the earth, holding back the winds, and another angel cries out that no harm may come until the servants of God have been sealed on their foreheads. John hears the number: one hundred forty-four thousand, twelve thousand from each of the tribes of Israel, and the tribes are named one by one.

Then he looks again, and the picture opens wide. There is “a great multitude which no man could count,” from every nation, tribe and language, standing before the throne in white robes with palm branches in their hands. They cry, “Salvation be to our God”. An elder asks John who they are and tells him they came out of the great suffering, the elder says, and God will “wipe away every tear from their eyes.”

Many scholars think John writes to churches under pressure, and this chapter is a pause between the sixth and seventh seals. First the sealed are counted, then a crowd beyond counting is seen. Christians differ over whether these are two groups or one, and over whether the tribes of Israel mean the people of Israel, the church or both. All agree that the scene is a promise to those who suffer: they are known, kept and finally comforted.

When the Lamb opens the seventh seal, nothing happens. There is “silence in heaven for about half an hour.” Then seven angels are given seven trumpets, and another angel stands at the golden altar with a censer. Much incense goes up before God with the prayers of the saints. The angel fills the censer with fire from the altar and throws it on the earth, and thunder, lightning and an earthquake follow.

Now the trumpets sound, one by one. Hail and fire mixed with blood burn a third of the earth. A burning mountain falls into the sea. A star called Wormwood turns a third of the waters bitter, and many die from them. A third of the sun, moon and stars goes dark. Then an eagle crosses the sky crying, “Woe! Woe! Woe” for the three trumpets still to come.

After the seals comes a new series, the trumpets. The damage is counted in thirds, so it is serious but not yet final. Many readers hear echoes of the plagues of Egypt (see Exodus 7 to 10) and of the prophets’ warnings. The chapter also joins the prayers of God’s people to the first act of judgment: the incense rises with their prayers before the fire is thrown. Christians differ on whether the trumpets describe past, future or recurring events.

The fifth angel sounds, and a fallen star is given the key to the pit of the abyss. He opens it, smoke pours out until the sun is dark, and locusts come out of the smoke with the power of scorpions. They may not harm the grass or the trees, only the people who do not have God’s seal on their foreheads, and only to torment them for five months. Their king is the angel of the abyss, named Abaddon in Hebrew and Apollyon in Greek.

The sixth angel sounds, and four angels bound at the Euphrates are set free. Armies of horsemen, two hundred million strong, kill a third of mankind with fire, smoke and sulfur. Then the chapter ends with a grim note: the rest of mankind “didn’t repent” of their idols or of their murders, sorceries, sexual immorality and thefts.

This is among the hardest chapters in the book, and it is a vision, full of symbols, not a forecast in plain speech. Christians read the locusts and the cavalry in different ways: as spiritual forces, as invading armies, as pictures of coming judgment. The text notes the limits set on the first plague, and it ends by saying that the survivors still did not turn.

A mighty angel comes down out of the sky, wrapped in a cloud, with a rainbow on his head and a face like the sun. One foot is on the sea and one on the land, and in his hand is a little open book. He cries out like a lion, and seven thunders answer. John is about to write down what they said, but a voice tells him, “Seal up the things which the seven thunders said, and don’t write them.”

The angel swears that there will be no more delay: when the seventh angel is about to sound, the mystery of God will be finished. Then John is told to take the little book and eat it. In his mouth it is “as sweet as honey”, but it turns his stomach bitter. The chapter closes with a charge: “You must prophesy again over many peoples, nations, languages, and kings.”

The chapter is an interlude between the sixth and seventh trumpets. John’s eating of a scroll echoes the prophet Ezekiel’s (see Ezekiel 2 and 3). Readers have often seen in the sweet and bitter taste the double experience of receiving God’s word: it is good to take in, and it brings a hard message to others. That some of what John heard was to stay sealed is a reminder that the book itself does not claim to say everything.

John is handed a reed and told to measure the temple, the altar and those who worship there, but to leave the outer court alone, for it has been given to the nations. Then God speaks of two witnesses, clothed in sackcloth, who will prophesy for one thousand two hundred sixty days. Fire comes from their mouths, and they have power over the sky and the waters. When their testimony is finished, the beast from the abyss kills them, and their bodies lie in the street of the great city while the earth’s peoples gloat and exchange gifts.

After three and a half days, the breath of life from God enters them. They stand, and a voice calls, “Come up here!” An earthquake follows. Then the seventh trumpet sounds, and heaven cries out, “The kingdom of the world has become the Kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ.”

Christians read this chapter in very different ways, and no single reading is settled. Some think the temple and the two witnesses refer to real people or events, past or future; others read them as symbols of the faithful church bearing witness in a hostile world. The text itself ties the two witnesses to the prophets’ lampstands and olive trees (see Zechariah 4). The chapter ends with the loudest declaration so far: the rule of the world belongs to God and his Christ.

“A great sign was seen in heaven”: a woman clothed with the sun, the moon under her feet, twelve stars on her head, crying out as she is about to give birth. Before her stands a huge red dragon with seven heads and ten horns, waiting to devour her child. But the child is born and caught up to God, and the woman flees to a place prepared for her in the wilderness.

War breaks out in the sky. Michael and his angels fight the dragon, who is thrown down to earth, the old serpent called the devil and Satan. A loud voice announces that the accuser has been defeated: “They overcame him because of the Lamb’s blood”. But on earth the dragon rages, and the woman is given the wings of a great eagle. The earth swallows the river the dragon sends after her, and the dragon goes off to make war on the rest of her offspring.

This chapter retells a great conflict in symbols, and Christians identify the woman in different ways: as Israel, as the church, as Mary, or as the whole people of God. The dragon is named plainly in the text as the old serpent, the devil and Satan, so readers often hear an echo of the serpent in Genesis 3. The victory it describes is won by the Lamb’s blood and by the faithful witness of believers, not by force of arms.

The dragon waits on the sand by the sea, and out of the sea comes a beast with ten horns and seven heads, like a leopard with the feet of a bear and the mouth of a lion. The dragon gives it his power and his throne. One of its heads seems fatally wounded, yet the wound heals, and the whole earth marvels. People worship the dragon and the beast, asking, “Who is like the beast? Who is able to make war with him?”

A second beast rises out of the earth with two horns like a lamb but a voice like a dragon. It works signs, makes an image of the first beast, and decrees that no one may buy or sell without its mark. The number is given as six hundred sixty-six. In the middle of it all the text speaks to the faithful: “Here is the endurance and the faith of the saints.”

Many scholars think the first readers heard in the first beast the power of Rome and its demand for worship, since the book is addressed to churches under pressure. Others see a figure still to come, and others a pattern that repeats in every age. The number is called “the number of a man”, and people through the centuries have proposed names for it. The text’s own concern is plain: those who refuse to worship the beast need endurance, and the book of life belongs to the Lamb.

On Mount Zion stands the Lamb, with one hundred forty-four thousand who have his name and his Father’s name written on their foreheads. A sound from heaven like many waters and like thunder fills the air, and they sing a new song that no one else can learn. Three angels fly with messages. The first carries an eternal Good News and cries that “the hour of his judgment has come.” The second announces that Babylon the great has fallen. The third warns those who worship the beast of the wine of God’s wrath.

Then a voice says, “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on”, for they rest from their labors. The chapter ends with a harvest: one like a son of man with a sickle reaps the earth, and an angel gathers the grapes of the earth and throws them into the winepress of God’s wrath.

The chapter sets two pictures against each other, a company that follows the Lamb and a world that follows the beast. Verse 4 calls the one hundred forty-four thousand virgins who were not defiled with women; many Christians read this as a picture of faithfulness to God, as the prophets often described idolatry as adultery, and not as a rule about marriage. The scenes of judgment are among the severest in the Bible, and Christians read them as a sign that God takes evil seriously.

John sees another great and marvelous sign in the sky: seven angels with the seven last plagues, for in them God’s wrath is finished. Before them lies something like a sea of glass mixed with fire, and standing beside it are those who overcame the beast, his image and the number of his name. They hold harps of God and sing the song of Moses and the song of the Lamb: “Great and marvelous are your works, Lord God, the Almighty!”

They praise God as King of the nations whose ways are righteous and true, and they say that all the nations will come and worship before him. Then the temple in heaven opens, and the seven angels come out in bright linen with golden sashes. One of the four living creatures gives them seven golden bowls full of God’s wrath, and smoke from God’s glory fills the temple so that no one can enter.

This short chapter is the doorway to the final series, the bowls, which fill the next chapter. The song of Moses points back to the song the Israelites sang after crossing the sea (see Exodus 15), and the sea of glass and fire recalls that rescue. Before the last plagues, the people who stood firm are seen safe on the far side, and they praise God’s justice. The smoke filling the temple echoes the moments when God’s glory filled the tabernacle (see Exodus 40).

A loud voice from the temple tells the seven angels, “Go and pour out the seven bowls of the wrath of God on the earth!” The first bowl brings painful sores on those who bear the beast’s mark. The second turns the sea to blood, and the third turns the rivers and springs to blood. The angel of the waters says that God’s judgments are true and righteous. The fourth bowl scorches people with heat, and they blaspheme God rather than turn. The fifth darkens the beast’s kingdom, and again they will not repent.

The sixth dries up the Euphrates, and three unclean spirits like frogs go out to gather the kings of the earth at a place called Harmagedon. In the middle comes a warning: “Behold, I come like a thief.” The seventh bowl is poured into the air, and a voice cries, “It is done!” Lightning, a great earthquake and enormous hailstones fall, and Babylon the great is divided into three parts.

The bowls echo the plagues of Egypt (see Exodus 7 to 10), but they are now aimed at the beast’s kingdom. The chapter returns three times to the same sad note: people do not repent. Harmagedon, the source of the later word Armageddon, is named in Hebrew in the text, and Christians disagree about where or when it is meant. As with other judgment scenes in Revelation, readers are asked to see the justice of God and the seriousness of evil.

One of the seven angels says to John, “Come here”, and promises to show him the judgment of the great prostitute who sits on many waters. John is carried in the Spirit into a wilderness, and there he sees a woman dressed in purple and scarlet, with gold and pearls and a golden cup in her hand, sitting on a scarlet beast with seven heads and ten horns. On her forehead a name is written: “MYSTERY, BABYLON THE GREAT”. She is drunk with the blood of the saints, and John wonders with great amazement.

The angel explains. The seven heads are seven mountains and also seven kings. The ten horns are ten kings who give their power to the beast. They will make war against the Lamb, “and the Lamb will overcome them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings”. The angel ends: the woman is the great city that reigns over the kings of the earth.

The text itself says the woman is a city, and many scholars think its first readers heard Rome, the city set on seven hills. Over the centuries other groups have tried to fit the woman to their enemies, and Christians disagree strongly with such uses; the image is of a power that corrupts and kills, not of a people or a faith. The chapter’s answer to this power comes quickly: the Lamb overcomes, and those with him are called, chosen and faithful.

An angel with great authority comes down, and the earth is lit with his glory. He cries, “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great” The city has become a haunt of demons and unclean birds, because the nations and the merchants of the earth grew rich from her luxury. Another voice from heaven calls out, “Come out of her, my people,” so that they will not share in her sins.

Then the mourners come. The kings of the earth, who lived with her in luxury, stand far away and weep as they see her smoke. The merchants and ship masters weep too, for no one buys their cargo any more. The list of that cargo runs from gold and pearls to wine and wheat, and ends with horses, chariots and “people’s bodies and souls.” In the end a mighty angel throws a millstone into the sea. Never again will music, craftsmen, lamplight or the voice of a bride and bridegroom be heard in her.

The chapter is a funeral song for a city, modeled on the prophets’ songs against Babylon and Tyre (see Isaiah 47, Jeremiah 50 and 51, and Ezekiel 27). Many scholars think the first readers heard in it a judgment on Roman power and its trade. The cargo list is striking because it ends with human beings, and the grief of the merchants is for their profits. For the faithful the call is to leave, and heaven is told to rejoice.

Heaven erupts. A great multitude cries out praise to God, because his judgments are true and righteous. The twenty-four elders and the four living creatures fall down and worship. Then comes the voice of a great multitude like many waters, announcing that the wedding of the Lamb has come, and his wife has made herself ready in bright, pure linen, which stands for the righteous acts of the saints. John is told to write that those invited to the wedding supper of the Lamb are blessed. He falls at the angel’s feet to worship, but the angel stops him: “Worship God”.

Then heaven opens on a white horse. Its rider is called Faithful and True, his eyes are a flame of fire, his robe is sprinkled with blood, and his name is “The Word of God.” Armies in white follow him. The beast and the kings of the earth gather to make war, but the beast and the false prophet are seized, and the rest are killed by the sword that comes out of the rider’s mouth.

The chapter holds a wedding and a war. Christians read the wedding supper as the final joy of God’s people, and the rider on the white horse as Christ. The sword comes from his mouth, which many readers take to mean that he wins by his word. Many readers take the violence of the later verses as symbolic language that echoes the prophets (see Isaiah 63). The angel’s refusal of John’s worship shows what the book most wants its readers to do: worship God alone.

An angel comes down from heaven with the key to the abyss and a great chain. He seizes the dragon, the old serpent, who is the devil and Satan, and binds him for a thousand years, shutting and sealing the abyss over him so that he deceives the nations no more. John sees thrones, and those who were beheaded for the testimony of Jesus come to life and reign with Christ for a thousand years. “This is the first resurrection.”

After the thousand years Satan is released and gathers the nations, Gog and Magog, to surround the camp of the saints, but fire from heaven devours them, and the devil is thrown into the lake of fire. Then John sees a great white throne. The dead stand before it, books are opened, and “the book of life” is opened too. They are judged by what they have done. Death and Hades give up their dead, and then Death and Hades are themselves thrown into the lake of fire.

Christians have read the thousand years in at least three main ways. Some expect a future reign of Christ on earth before the end; some think it describes the present age of the church; some expect a golden age brought by the gospel before Christ returns. The chapter is clear on what ends: the dragon is defeated, the dead are judged, and death itself is destroyed. The great white throne is among the most solemn scenes in the Bible, and it ends with evil gone.

The vision turns from judgment to home. John sees a new heaven and a new earth, for the first have passed away, and the sea is no more. The holy city, New Jerusalem, comes down out of heaven like a bride prepared for her husband. A loud voice announces, “Behold, God’s dwelling is with people”. God himself will be with them and wipe away every tear. “Death will be no more”. The one on the throne says, “Behold, I am making all things new.”

An angel carries John to a mountain and shows him the city. It has a great wall of jasper with twelve gates, each a single pearl, and the names of the twelve tribes of Israel are on the gates and the names of the twelve apostles on the foundations. The city is pure gold like clear glass, and it is built square. There is no temple, because the Lord God and the Lamb are its temple. It needs no sun or moon, for God’s glory lights it. Its gates are never shut, and the nations bring their glory into it.

After the long visions of judgment, Revelation closes with a picture of God making his home with people, the reverse of the exile from the garden in Genesis 3. Christians read the city as a real place, as a symbol of God’s people, or as both. The measurements are in twelves, and the city is a perfect cube, like the holy of holies (see 1 Kings 6). Verse 8 names those whose part is in the lake of fire, which many readers take as a sober counterpart to the invitation to the thirsty in verse 6.

The river of the water of life runs clear as crystal from the throne of God and of the Lamb, down the middle of the city’s street. On both sides stands the tree of life, bearing twelve kinds of fruit and yielding it every month, and its leaves are “for the healing of the nations.” There is no more curse, no night, and no need of lamp or sun. God’s servants will see his face.

Then the angel tells John these words are faithful and true, and a voice says that he is coming soon. John falls down to worship the angel, and again he is stopped. Worship is for God only. The chapter closes with invitations and a warning. The Spirit and the bride say to come, and whoever is thirsty may take the water of life freely. No one may add to or take away from this book. The last words of the Bible’s final book are a prayer: “Yes, come, Lord Jesus!” and a blessing of grace.

This is the final chapter of Revelation and of the Christian Bible. The river, the tree of life and the end of the curse look back to the first chapters of Genesis (see Genesis 2 and 3), so the story ends where it began, with God and people together. The warning against adding to or taking away from the book is aimed at this book, not at the whole Bible.
